itineraryStops.name: Pickup (your downtown Busan hotel)
itineraryStops.description:
Door-to-door pickup at your hotel in central Busan, between **09:00 and 10:00**. Your exact time is confirmed by WhatsApp the evening before, once the driver has the day's hotel list and can order the run efficiently — guests on the Haeundae side are usually collected last, because the coach leaves the city heading northeast toward Gijang-gun for the first stop.

The supported area covers the central hotel clusters: **Seomyeon**, **Nampo-dong / Busan Station**, and **Haeundae / Marine City**. If your hotel sits outside that area, the guide names the nearest meeting point when the booking is confirmed.

Please wait in the lobby 5 minutes before your confirmed time. Transit from the last pickup to Haedong Yonggungsa is about 30–40 minutes depending on traffic.
highlights: Door-to-door pickup at central Busan hotels, 09:00–10:00
Exact time confirmed by WhatsApp the evening before
Coach is small-group (max ~14 pax)
Printed Korean-English itinerary card distributed at pickup
timeUsed: Hotel pickups across central Busan (~40 min)
Drive northeast to Gijang-gun (~20 min)
itineraryStops.whyOnRoute: Hotel pickup removes the morning transfer entirely — no early subway ride, no hunting for the right station exit. The run is ordered west→east so the coach finishes near Haeundae and leaves the city already pointed at Gijang and the day's first stop.

itineraryStops.whyOnRoute: **The route's iconic opener — Busan's most-photographed temple in its quiet window.** The 10:20 arrival lands before the major tour-bus surge (typically from 11:00), so the 108-stair descent and the Haesu Gwaneum viewpoint are still walkable without queuing. Its Gijang cliff-top location also starts the day at the route's far northeast point, so everything after flows one-way down the coast — Cheongsapo next, then the capsule ride toward the city — with no backtracking.

itineraryStops.description:
**Haedong Yonggungsa (해동 용궁사) — Korea's most famous seaside Buddhist temple** — perches on the rocky cliffs of Gijang-gun on Busan's northeastern coast, one of the very few major Korean temples NOT set in the mountains. Originally founded in **1376 during the Goryeo Dynasty by the great Buddhist teacher Naong Hyegeun (나옹 혜근, 1320-1376)** — a royal consultant and master who would help shape Korean Buddhism into the early Joseon era. 

Per legend, Naong was practicing asceticism at Bunhwangsa Temple in Gyeongju during a national drought; the East Sea god appeared to him in a dream and told him that building a temple on Bongrae Mountain (the original name of this seaside cliff) would restore the kingdom's prosperity. 

Naong founded the temple and named it **Bomunsa**, dedicated to Gwanseum-bosal (관세음보살, the Bodhisattva of Compassion). The temple was destroyed in the **Japanese Imjin Invasion of 1592** and lay in ruins for over 300 years until **Monk Ungang of Tongdosa Temple began reconstruction in the early 1930s**. 

The current name, **Haedong Yonggungsa (Korean Dragon Palace Temple)**, dates only to **1974** — when Head Monk Jeong-am, during a 100-day prayer (jeong-geon kido), had a vision of the Goddess of Mercy descending on the back of a dragon, emanating multicolor light. 

The temple was renamed to honor this vision. The visit follows the temple's signature processional path: through the row of **12 Sibiji-shin (Twelve Zodiac Generals)** at the entry plaza, past the **7-story 'No-Accident Pagoda'** (where drivers leave coin offerings under a stone wheel-shrine), down the famous **108 stone stairs** (representing the 108 delusions of the Buddhist mind) through a small bamboo grove, and out onto the seaside terraces and Daeungjeon main hall. 

The **Haesu Gwaneum Daebul** (Sea-Goddess of Mercy statue) on the upper cliff is the most photographed view, framing both the temple rooftops and the East Sea. 

Hours **04:30-19:20 daily, last entry 18:50, FREE admission**. **Buddha's Birthday (May)** brings Yeondunhoe lantern festival displays.

visitBasics.walking: Moderate — 108 steps through pine grove, multiple seaside terraces and stairs

itineraryStops.name: Cheongsapo Daritdol Observatory (glass skywalk)
itineraryStops.description: The **Cheongsapo Daritdol Observatory (청사포 다릿돌전망대)** is a **72.5-meter skywalk curving out over the sea about 20 meters above the water**, opened in August 2017 on the coastal cliff between Cheongsapo and Songjeong. Its name comes from the **daritdol — the five 'stepping-stone' reef rocks** that dot the sea below the deck, said to step toward the horizon like a bridge. The far section of the deck floor is **glass**, with shoe covers provided to protect (and trust!) the panes as the swell rolls beneath your feet. Admission is **free**. Back at the village, the **Cheongsapo Twin Lighthouses** (one red, one white) and the little station crosswalk made famous by its Slam-Dunk-style anime frame are a short stroll away.
highlights: **72.5-m skywalk, ~20 m above the sea** — opened August 2017, FREE
Named for the five **daritdol 'stepping-stone' reefs** visible below the deck
**Glass-floor section** at the seaward end (shoe covers provided)
**Cheongsapo Twin Lighthouses** (red + white) a short stroll away
Cheongsapo is one of Busan's **eight scenic views** — a working fishing village
Anime-famous station crosswalk photo spot
timeUsed: Coach drop-off + walk to the skywalk entrance (~5 min)
Skywalk walk-out + glass-floor section (~20 min)
Twin lighthouses / crosswalk photo stroll (~10 min)
Reassemble for the capsule station (~5 min)
itineraryStops.whyOnRoute: **The free thrill between the temple and the capsule.** Daritdol gives the day its over-the-sea moment — a glass floor with swell rolling underneath — without a ticket, and it sits directly on the Cheongsapo cliff so it chains into the Sky Capsule boarding just minutes away. Seeing the coastline from the fixed skywalk first makes the moving capsule view read differently ten minutes later.

smartNotes.photo: Shoot down through the glass at the daritdol reefs; the deck's curve from the shore path gives the best wide shot
smartNotes.facilities: Cafes and seafood stalls in Cheongsapo village below

convenience.parking: Coach stop at Cheongsapo village; short walk to the deck

itineraryStops.name: Haeundae Blueline Park Sky Capsule (Cheongsapo → Mipo)
itineraryStops.description: The **Sky Capsule** is the signature ride of **Haeundae Blueline Park**, the 2020 eco-redevelopment of the disused Donghae Nambu coastal railway: **pastel 4-seat cabins gliding 2.3 km along an elevated rail 7–10 meters above the coastline** between Cheongsapo and Mipo, with the sea on one side the whole way (~30 minutes). We board at **Cheongsapo and ride toward Mipo**, where the coach is already waiting — so the ride doubles as the day's transfer down the coast. **The capsule ticket is optional and chosen at booking**: with the ticket-included option we pre-reserve capsules for your group (pricing is per capsule: about ₩30,000 for 2 / ₩39,000 for 3 / ₩44,000 for 4, one-way); with the base option you can walk the **free Green Railway boardwalk** — the award-winning 2.3 km wooden coastal path under the same rail — or simply ride the coach to Mipo.
highlights: **Pastel 4-seat capsules on an elevated coastal rail** — Blueline Park's signature ride (opened 2020)
**Cheongsapo → Mipo, 2.3 km / ~30 min**, sea views the whole way
**Ticket included or excluded — your choice at booking** (per-capsule pricing ≈ ₩30,000 for 2 / ₩39,000 for 3 / ₩44,000 for 4, one-way)
Non-riders: **free Green Railway boardwalk** along the same coast, or the coach to Mipo
The ride ends where lunch begins — Mipo is a short walk from Haeundae's food streets
Runs in normal rain; pauses only in high wind
timeUsed: Boarding at Cheongsapo station (~15 min)
Sky Capsule ride Cheongsapo → Mipo (~35 min)
itineraryStops.whyOnRoute: **The ride that is also the transfer.** Boarding at Cheongsapo right after the skywalk means the capsule carries you down the exact coastline you just looked out over — and it deposits you at Mipo, where the coach and the lunch streets are already waiting. Nothing about the day detours for it: skip the ticket and the coach or the free boardwalk cover the same leg.

smartNotes.tip: Sunset and weekend slots sell out 1–2 weeks ahead — choose the ticket-included option at booking and we reserve them for you
smartNotes.photo: Sit on the sea side (right side heading to Mipo); the curve past Dalmaji Tunnel is the signature frame
smartNotes.facilities: Cafes and convenience store at Mipo plaza; ticket kiosks at both stations

convenience.parking: Coach meets the group at Mipo station plaza
convenience.restroom: At both Cheongsapo and Mipo stations

Fueling up here sets up the afternoon's two hillside villages, where the walking is at its most vertical.

Typical guide-recommended options: **dwaeji-gukbap (돼지국밥)** — Busan's signature pork-broth rice soup born in the Korean-War refugee era (~₩10,000), **milmyeon** cold wheat noodles, or a harborside seafood table. Lunch is not included (≈ ₩10,000–15,000), so you can pick what suits your appetite and budget.

itineraryStops.name: Haeundae Beach
itineraryStops.description:
**Haeundae Beach (해운대해수욕장)** is Korea's best-known stretch of sand — about **1.5 km** of shoreline curving between Dongbaekseom island at the west end and Mipo at the east, backed by the Marine City skyline. The Sky Capsule sets you down at Mipo, which is simply the eastern end of this beach, so the stop costs the day no extra driving.

Twenty minutes is a photo-and-toes stop, not a swim: walk out onto the sand, shoot the skyline, and rejoin the coach. In July and August the beach is at its busiest and the parasol rows are up; the rest of the year it is wide, quiet and walkable. Free, open at all hours.
highlights: **Korea's most famous beach** — ~1.5 km of sand, FREE and open 24h
Marine City skyline backdrop from the water's edge
Dongbaekseom island and Nurimaru APEC House at the far west end
Directly at Mipo, where the Sky Capsule ride ends — no extra transfer
timeUsed: Walk onto the sand from Mipo (~5 min)
Beach and skyline photos (~10 min)
Reassemble at the coach (~5 min)
itineraryStops.whyOnRoute: The capsule lands at Mipo, which is the beach's eastern end — so Busan's most famous view is a five-minute walk away and costs the day nothing. It is deliberately short: enough to stand on the sand and photograph the skyline before the afternoon turns to the hillside villages.

itineraryStops.description:
**Gamcheon Culture Village (감천문화마을)** — nicknamed both **'Korea's Machu Picchu'** and **'Korea's Santorini'** — is a hillside neighborhood in Saha-gu, west Busan, whose pastel-painted houses cascade down in stepped rows over the slope. 

The settlement began in the **1920s-1930s** when the Busan administration relocated working-class residents away from the port. The village's character was set in **1955** when **~800 families (about 4,000 people) of the Taegeukdo religious community** — a uniquely Korean syncretic religion blending Buddhist, Confucian, and yin-yang elements, founded by **Jo Cheol-je** during the Japanese colonial period — settled here as Korean War refugees fleeing the North. 

The Taegeukdo philosophy of '**allowing others to prosper**' directly shaped the village's most distinctive feature: houses are intentionally tiered so that **no roof blocks the view of the house behind it**, with the entire community visible to the sky and the sea. Gamcheon remained one of Busan's poorest neighborhoods until **2009**, when the Korean Ministry of Culture launched the **'Dreaming of Machu Picchu in Busan'** public-art revitalization project, followed by the **'Miro Miro' (maze) project in 2010** — adding 22+ commissioned murals, sculptures, and art installations including the iconic **'Little Prince and Fox' bench** at the Sky Garden viewpoint. 

Gamcheon won the **2012 UN-HABITAT Asian Townscape Award** and now welcomes **~1.4 million visitors annually**. The visit follows the village's signature stamp-map walking route: from the entrance at the **Tourist Information Center**, up to **Sky Garden viewpoint** for the panoramic rainbow-roof shot, then down through the labyrinthine alleys past murals, hanbok rental shops, craft workshops, and small cafes. 

**The village is a living residential community** — quiet voices required, no drones, no flash photography into homes, and rubbish carried out. 

Hours **09:00-18:00 Mar-Oct / 09:00-17:00 Nov-Feb (info center)**; **village itself open 24h, FREE entry**.

visitBasics.hours: Daily 09:00–18:00 (Mar–Oct) / 09:00–17:00 (Nov–Feb); some shops/cafes keep their own hours
visitBasics.walking: Strenuous — very steep alleys and stairs; not stroller- or wheelchair-friendly in many sections
visitBasics.admission: Free village entry; optional Stamp Map ≈ 2,000 KRW

itineraryStops.name: Dakbatgol Mural Village & Wish-Stairs Monorail
itineraryStops.description: **Dakbatgol (닥밭골)** is a hillside village in Busan's Seo-gu whose name remembers the **paper-mulberry (dak) fields** that once supplied Korea's traditional hanji paper-makers. Like Gamcheon it climbs a steep slope in tight lanes — but it never became a tour-bus stop, so its **mural alleys, hanji-motif artwork, and lookout points stay quiet and local**, laundry lines and all. The village's landmark is the **'wish stairs' (소망계단)** — a long, steep stair street painted with murals — and the **free incline monorail** that glides beside it, installed so the village's elderly residents could reach their homes; visitors ride it too, turning the steepest climb of the afternoon into a slow-motion viewpoint. It is the deliberately human-scale counterpoint to Gamcheon's fame, ten minutes before drop-off territory.
highlights: **Quiet mural village** — Gamcheon's local counterpart with almost no crowds
Named for the **paper-mulberry (dak) fields** of Busan's hanji paper heritage
**'Wish stairs' (소망계단)** — a steep mural stair street
**Free incline monorail** beside the stairs — built for village elders, open to visitors
Hillside lookouts over the old harbor quarter
FREE admission; a genuinely lived-in neighborhood — keep voices low
timeUsed: Coach drop-off + mural lane walk (~10 min)
Wish-stairs monorail ride up + lookout (~10 min)
Descent + photo time (~5 min)
Reassemble at coach (~5 min)
itineraryStops.whyOnRoute: **The quiet closer the buses skip.** After Gamcheon's crowds, Dakbatgol shows the same hillside Busan at living volume — murals, wish stairs, and a monorail that does the climbing. It closes the villages chapter ten minutes from the Nampo drop-off zone, so the day ends deep in local texture rather than in traffic.

smartNotes.tip: This is a lived-in village, not a theme park — keep voices low in the alleys and don't photograph into open doorways
smartNotes.photo: Shoot the wish stairs from the bottom with the monorail track running beside; the top lookout frames the harbor quarter
smartNotes.facilities: Small cafes near the entrance; more options at Nampo-dong after drop-off

convenience.parking: Coach stop at the village entrance
convenience.restroom: Public restroom near the village entrance

staticQuestions.answer: Moderate-to-challenging in short bursts: 108 stairs down and up at Yonggungsa, flat glass skywalk at Daritdol, mostly flat at the capsule stations, hillside lanes at Gamcheon, and stairs at Dakbatgol — where the free monorail does the climbing for you. staticQuestions.question: Is this suitable for children or seniors?
staticQuestions.answer: Yes for most active travelers. Kids love the glass floor and the capsule; the Dakbatgol monorail spares the steepest climb. The Yonggungsa stairs and Gamcheon slopes are the two demanding sections — take them slowly and skip side alleys as needed.

staticQuestions.question: How is this different from the Busan Top Attractions day tour?

This small-group route doubles down on the coast and the villages: a dedicated Daritdol skywalk stop, the Sky Capsule ride with an included-ticket option, and the quiet Dakbatgol mural village that big buses skip.

itineraryStops.description:
**Haedong Yonggungsa (해동 용궁사) — Korea's most famous seaside Buddhist temple** — perches on the rocky cliffs of Gijang-gun on Busan's northeastern coast, one of the very few major Korean temples NOT set in the mountains. Originally founded in **1376 during the Goryeo Dynasty by the great Buddhist teacher Naong Hyegeun (나옹 혜근, 1320-1376)** — a royal consultant and master who would help shape Korean Buddhism into the early Joseon era. 

Per legend, Naong was practicing asceticism at Bunhwangsa Temple in Gyeongju during a national drought; the East Sea god appeared to him in a dream and told him that building a temple on Bongrae Mountain (the original name of this seaside cliff) would restore the kingdom's prosperity. 

Naong founded the temple and named it **Bomunsa**, dedicated to Gwanseum-bosal (관세음보살, the Bodhisattva of Compassion). The temple was destroyed in the **Japanese Imjin Invasion of 1592** and lay in ruins for over 300 years until **Monk Ungang of Tongdosa Temple began reconstruction in the early 1930s**. 

The current name, **Haedong Yonggungsa (Korean Dragon Palace Temple)**, dates only to **1974** — when Head Monk Jeong-am, during a 100-day prayer (jeong-geon kido), had a vision of the Goddess of Mercy descending on the back of a dragon, emanating multicolor light. 

The temple was renamed to honor this vision. The visit follows the temple's signature processional path: through the row of **12 Sibiji-shin (Twelve Zodiac Generals)** at the entry plaza, past the **7-story 'No-Accident Pagoda'** (where drivers leave coin offerings under a stone wheel-shrine), down the famous **108 stone stairs** (representing the 108 delusions of the Buddhist mind) through a small bamboo grove, and out onto the seaside terraces and Daeungjeon main hall. 

The **Haesu Gwaneum Daebul** (Sea-Goddess of Mercy statue) on the upper cliff is the most photographed view, framing both the temple rooftops and the East Sea. 

Hours **04:30-19:20 daily, last entry 18:50, FREE admission**. **Buddha's Birthday (May)** brings Yeondunhoe lantern festival displays.

itineraryStops.description: The **Cheongsapo Daritdol Observatory (청사포 다릿돌전망대)** is a **72.5-meter skywalk curving out over the sea about 20 meters above the water**, opened in August 2017 on the coastal cliff between Cheongsapo and Songjeong. Its name comes from the **daritdol — the five 'stepping-stone' reef rocks** that dot the sea below the deck, said to step toward the horizon like a bridge. The far section of the deck floor is **glass**, with shoe covers provided to protect (and trust!) the panes as the swell rolls beneath your feet. Admission is **free**. Back at the village, the **Cheongsapo Twin Lighthouses** (one red, one white) and the little station crosswalk made famous by its Slam-Dunk-style anime frame are a short stroll away.

itineraryStops.description:
**Gamcheon Culture Village (감천문화마을)** — nicknamed both **'Korea's Machu Picchu'** and **'Korea's Santorini'** — is a hillside neighborhood in Saha-gu, west Busan, whose pastel-painted houses cascade down in stepped rows over the slope. 

The settlement began in the **1920s-1930s** when the Busan administration relocated working-class residents away from the port. The village's character was set in **1955** when **~800 families (about 4,000 people) of the Taegeukdo religious community** — a uniquely Korean syncretic religion blending Buddhist, Confucian, and yin-yang elements, founded by **Jo Cheol-je** during the Japanese colonial period — settled here as Korean War refugees fleeing the North. 

The Taegeukdo philosophy of '**allowing others to prosper**' directly shaped the village's most distinctive feature: houses are intentionally tiered so that **no roof blocks the view of the house behind it**, with the entire community visible to the sky and the sea. Gamcheon remained one of Busan's poorest neighborhoods until **2009**, when the Korean Ministry of Culture launched the **'Dreaming of Machu Picchu in Busan'** public-art revitalization project, followed by the **'Miro Miro' (maze) project in 2010** — adding 22+ commissioned murals, sculptures, and art installations including the iconic **'Little Prince and Fox' bench** at the Sky Garden viewpoint. 

Gamcheon won the **2012 UN-HABITAT Asian Townscape Award** and now welcomes **~1.4 million visitors annually**. The visit follows the village's signature stamp-map walking route: from the entrance at the **Tourist Information Center**, up to **Sky Garden viewpoint** for the panoramic rainbow-roof shot, then down through the labyrinthine alleys past murals, hanbok rental shops, craft workshops, and small cafes. 

**The village is a living residential community** — quiet voices required, no drones, no flash photography into homes, and rubbish carried out. 

Hours **09:00-18:00 Mar-Oct / 09:00-17:00 Nov-Feb (info center)**; **village itself open 24h, FREE entry**.

itineraryStops.name: Dakbatgol Mural Village & Wish-Stairs Monorail
itineraryStops.description: **Dakbatgol (닥밭골)** is a hillside village in Busan's Seo-gu whose name remembers the **paper-mulberry (dak) fields** that once supplied Korea's traditional hanji paper-makers. Like Gamcheon it climbs a steep slope in tight lanes — but it never became a tour-bus stop, so its **mural alleys, hanji-motif artwork, and lookout points stay quiet and local**, laundry lines and all. The village's landmark is the **'wish stairs' (소망계단)** — a long, steep stair street painted with murals — and the **free incline monorail** that glides beside it, installed so the village's elderly residents could reach their homes; visitors ride it too, turning the steepest climb of the afternoon into a slow-motion viewpoint. It is the deliberately human-scale counterpoint to Gamcheon's fame, ten minutes before drop-off territory.

routeShapeIntro.title: How this Busan day moves
routeShapeIntro.subtitle: East coast first: the seaside temple in its quiet morning window, then the Cheongsapo cluster — glass skywalk, twin lighthouses — where the Sky Capsule ride itself becomes the transfer down the coast to Mipo. After lunch and a short stop on Haeundae Beach the day crosses to Busan's west hillsides for two villages in two moods: Gamcheon's world-famous color, then Dakbatgol's quiet murals, where a free monorail glides up the 'wish stairs'. Central drop-offs close the loop, 09:00 to about 18:20.

staticQuestions.answer: Sunset and weekend slots sell out 1–2 weeks ahead. If you choose the ticket-included option we handle the reservation for your group when the booking is confirmed. Same-day kiosk tickets are possible on quiet weekdays but not guaranteed.

staticQuestions.question: How much walking and how steep is it?
staticQuestions.answer: Moderate-to-challenging in short bursts: 108 stairs down and up at Yonggungsa, flat glass skywalk at Daritdol, mostly flat at the capsule stations, hillside lanes at Gamcheon, and stairs at Dakbatgol — where the free monorail does the climbing for you. Total on-foot distance is about 4–5 km.

staticQuestions.question: Is this suitable for children or seniors?
staticQuestions.answer: Yes for most active travelers. Kids love the glass floor and the capsule; the Dakbatgol monorail spares the steepest climb. The Yonggungsa stairs and Gamcheon slopes are the two demanding sections — take them slowly and skip side alleys as needed.

staticQuestions.question: How is this different from the Busan Top Attractions day tour?
staticQuestions.answer: Same operator, different focus. Top Attractions covers the classic city sweep (UN Memorial Cemetery, Jagalchi Market). This small-group route doubles down on the coast and the villages: a dedicated Daritdol skywalk stop, the Sky Capsule ride with an included-ticket option, and the quiet Dakbatgol mural village that big buses skip.

staticQuestions.question: Where do you pick up and drop off?

staticQuestions.question: What happens if it rains?
staticQuestions.answer: The day runs rain or shine. The capsule and monorail operate in normal rain (they pause only in high wind), the skywalk provides shoe covers, and village lanes stay walkable with an umbrella. Heavy weather may shorten outdoor time at the temple terraces.
